claim: A typical cause of drug-induced cardiac repolarization prolongation is the inhibition of the inward rectifying potassium channel (hERG or human ether-a-go-go related gene encoded by KCNH2).
source: A typical cause is the inhibition of the inward rectifying potassium channel (hERG or human ether-a-go-go related gene encoded by KCNH2) (Kannankeril et al., 2010; Roden, 2008a)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kannankeril et al., 2010 and Roden, 2008a

claim: hERG inhibition results in the prolongation of the repolarization time and induces an increase of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram.
source: A typical cause is the inhibition of the inward rectifying potassium channel (hERG or human ether-a-go-go related gene encoded by KCNH2) (Kannankeril et al., 2010; Roden, 2008a), which results in the prolongation of the repolarization time and induces an increase of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kannankeril et al., 2010 and Roden, 2008a

claim: Drug-induced long QT is a major cause of drug withdrawal or of premature termination during development.
source: Eventually, diLQT is a major cause of drug withdrawal or of premature termination during development (Fermini and Fossa, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fermini and Fossa, 2003

claim: Regulatory agencies require that new drug candidates be systematically screened for hERG inhibition in animal models or in heterologous over-expression cellular systems.
source: Regulatory agencies require that new drug candidates be systematically screened for hERG inhibition in animal models or in heterologous over-expression cellular systems (Sager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sager et al., 2014

claim: hERG screening remains suboptimal and has a poor positive predictive value for subsequent proarrhythmia risk due to species-dependent differences of cardiac electrophysiology and the failure of heterologous systems to express all cardiac proteins.
source: Because of species-dependent differences of cardiac electrophysiology and the failure of heterologous systems to express all cardiac proteins, hERG screening however remains suboptimal and has a poor positive predictive value for subsequent proarrhythmia risk (Gintant, 2011; Giorgi et al., 2010; Sager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gintant, 2011; Giorgi et al., 2010; Sager et al., 2014

claim: Less than 10% of patients exposed to QT-prolonging drugs actually develop drug-induced long QT.
source: Previous studies in the general population have shown that a small proportion (i.e., less than 10%) of patients exposed to QT-prolonging drugs actually develop diLQT (Behr and Roden, 2013; Kannankeril et al., 2010; Soyka et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Behr and Roden, 2013; Kannankeril et al., 2010; Soyka et al., 1990

claim: First-degree relatives of patients with drug-induced long QT have a higher propensity to develop drug-induced repolarization abnormalities.
source: Different observations support the existence of a genetic determinism to diLQT including the higher propensity to develop drug-induced repolarization abnormalities in first-degree relatives of patients with diLQT (Kannankeril et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kannankeril et al., 2005

claim: Drug-induced long QT has similarity to the congenital form of the long QT syndrome (LQTS), a rare inherited cardiac disorder.
source: Different observations support the existence of a genetic determinism to diLQT including the higher propensity to develop drug-induced repolarization abnormalities in first-degree relatives of patients with diLQT (Kannankeril et al., 2005) and the similarity to the congenital form of the long QT syndrome (LQTS), a rare inherited cardiac disorder (Moss and Robinson, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moss and Robinson, 1992

claim: Multiple rare mutations with marked effects in genes encoding ion channels underlie congenital LQTS.

evidence: Supported by citation to Cerrone and Priori, 2011

claim: Candidate gene screening studies in large cohorts of patients with drug-induced long QT have reported a small prevalence (from 10 to 15%) of mutations in the known LQTS genes.

claim: QT prolongation can be induced by mutations in many genes that occupy a substantial region of the human interactome and contain many drug targets.

evidence: Supported by citation to Berger et al., 2010

claim: Drug-induced long QT is probably driven by the additive effect of common genetic variants that reduce the cardiac repolarization reserve.
